implementation_notes: Ruby makes immutability a per-object property: Object#freeze marks an object frozen so later mutation raises FrozenError, the magic comment # frozen_string_literal: true freezes every string literal in the file at parse time and makes identical literals share one object, and Ruby 3.2's Data.define builds immutable value classes with a generated initializer, equality, hash and #with as the wither - that replaces the hand-written value class whose initialize ends with freeze. freeze is shallow: a frozen array or hash still allows mutation of the objects it holds, so nested structures must be frozen level by level, and Ractor sharing requires the whole graph to be frozen and shareable. The classic approach is still justified when the object must remain a mutable Struct for a framework and is frozen only in a copy at the boundary.
code_sketch:
# frozen_string_literal: true
Measure = Data.define(:amount, :unit) do
  def with_amount(value) = with(amount: value)     # returns a new frozen instance
end

distance = Measure.new(100, 'km')
faster   = distance.with_amount(120)               # distance is still 100 'km'
CONFIG   = { ports: [8080].freeze }.freeze         # freeze each level: freeze is shallow
pitfalls: freeze is shallow: a frozen hash or array still lets you mutate the objects inside it, so nested shared structures must be frozen recursively.
dup returns an unfrozen copy while clone preserves frozen state (clone(freeze: false) overrides it), a subtle source of accidentally mutable copies.
Objects are only shareable with Ractors when the whole graph is frozen; Ractor.shareable? is the check, and freezing after publication has already raced.
A frozen object used as a Hash key still needs stable hash and eql?; nested mutable state breaks lookups even though the key itself is frozen.
